target_strain: E. faecium 17OM39 (BV-BRC 1352.1047) vs marketed probiotic T110 (BV-BRC 1344042.3)
verdict_context: PARTIAL — safety leaf-claims (C3 AMR, C4 virulence) reproduce; genome-stability MGE claim (C5) does not reproduce on public BV-BRC RASTtk annotation and is confounded by draft-vs-finished assembly status; core-genome phylogeny (C6) untested.

questions.q: What is the minimum genomic 'safe-strain' criterion for a candidate E. faecium probiotic — i.e. which specific VF/AMR gene absences, plus which clade-B markers, are sufficient (not just necessary) to distinguish a probiotic-candidate isolate from a hospital-adapted pathogen at the sequence level alone?
questions.basis: The paper argues 17OM39 is safe because it lacks vanA/vanB, canonical tet, Esp, cytolysin, gelatinase, aggregation substance, and collagen adhesin. We reproduced most absences (§4.2, §4.3 of REPORT.md) and even found that T110 — a MARKETED probiotic — carries the Cna collagen adhesin that 17OM39 lacks. So the paper's own comparator violates the strictest reading of its own safety criteria. This exposes an unresolved question: is there a defensible, published gene-absence panel (EFSA-QPS-style but sequence-level) that a candidate probiotic must clear, or is the current standard still ad-hoc per paper?
next_steps: Systematic review of EFSA QPS assessments for E. faecium (all rejected — EFSA does NOT grant QPS to E. faecium as a species); extract the exact genomic/phenotypic disqualifiers cited.

Curate a candidate safe-strain gene-absence panel from Freitas et al., Palmer et al., Lebreton et al. clade-A/B papers and re-score 17OM39, T110, and 10+ clinical E. faecium isolates against it using abricate + custom HMMs.
Publish the panel as a versioned YAML (fields: gene, source_DB, min_identity, min_coverage, rationale, clade-A frequency, clade-B frequency) so future 'safe strain' claims are auditable.

questions.q: The paper's safety argument is entirely genomic (gene presence/absence). What in-vitro and in-vivo phenotypic assays would need to accompany the genomic panel to make a strain-safety claim clinically defensible, and does 17OM39 have any published phenotypic data (bile/acid/salt tolerance survival curves, Caco-2 adhesion, hemolysis on blood agar, gelatinase plate assay, Galleria mellonella LD50, murine colonization)?
questions.basis: REPORT.md §4.5 shows 17OM39 has 3 bile-salt-hydrolase CDS, 9 bacteriocin/enterocin CDS, and 13 sortase A anchors — genomic potential for probiotic function. The paper (per §1 of REPORT.md) does not couple this to phenotypic validation, and our replication had no way to test phenotype from BV-BRC data alone. Without an in-vitro/in-vivo layer, 'lacks virulence genes' is not the same as 'is non-pathogenic in a host'.
next_steps: Literature scan (PubMed + Europe PMC) for any follow-up phenotypic characterization of strain 17OM39 since 2018.

If none exists, design a minimal 'strain-safety phenotypic panel' (bile 0.3%/pH 2.5/NaCl 6.5% survival, blood-agar hemolysis, gelatin liquefaction, Galleria LD50, in-vivo persistence in a mouse model) and estimate cost/timeline.
Cross-reference to any commercial probiotic containing 17OM39 (regulatory dossiers would contain the missing phenotypic data).

questions.q: Does 17OM39 actually sit in clade B (community/commensal) rather than clade A1 (hospital-adapted CC17), and can this be shown independently of the paper's own Roary tree — i.e. using MLST + core-genome ANI + Lebreton-clade-diagnostic SNPs against a modern reference panel of ~200 E. faecium genomes?
questions.basis: The paper's C6 claim (17OM39 clusters with T110 on the core-genome tree) implies 17OM39 is on the commensal/probiotic side of the E. faecium A/B split. REPORT.md §5 explicitly did NOT re-test C6 (needs Roary/PhyloPhlAn). Clade assignment is the single most important sequence-level indicator of probiotic-vs-pathogen risk for E. faecium (Lebreton et al. 2013 mBio; Palmer et al. 2012 mBio), so leaving it untested leaves the paper's central claim un-replicated.
next_steps: Run mlst v2 on 17OM39, T110, and 20 clade-A references (Aus0004, TX16, DO, U0317, etc.) + 20 clade-B references; confirm ST and CC17 status.
Compute fastANI 17OM39 vs the two clade centroids; report % ANI to each.

Extract Lebreton clade-diagnostic SNP set (or equivalent Raven et al. panel) and call clade B vs A1 vs A2 for 17OM39; publish alongside a Roary/PhyloPhlAn tree with bootstrap support at the (17OM39, T110) node.

questions.q: Are the bile / acid / salt tolerance genes (choloylglycine hydrolase / BSH, F0F1-ATPase, gadB, glutamate decarboxylase, opuA/BC osmoprotectant transporters, dltABCD teichoic-acid alanylation) conserved between 17OM39, T110, and a broader set of E. faecium probiotic candidates at both presence/absence AND sequence-similarity level, or does the paper's 'probiotic gene toolkit' actually vary meaningfully across candidates in ways that would predict differential gut-survival?
questions.basis: REPORT.md §4.5 shows 17OM39 and T110 have equivalent counts of bile salt hydrolase (3/3), bacteriocins (9 vs 13), and sortase A (13 vs 9). But count-parity ≠ functional-parity: BSH sequence variants have very different substrate specificities (glyco- vs tauro-conjugated bile acids), and bacteriocin gene counts include silent/pseudogene ORFs. The paper treats 'has bile salt hydrolase' as binary; the biology is not binary.
next_steps: Pull BSH, gadB, F0F1-ATPase-alpha, dltA, opuA amino-acid sequences from 17OM39, T110, and 20 other E. faecium genomes (probiotic + commensal + clinical); align + build gene trees.
Ask whether 17OM39's BSH clusters with the glyco-BSH or tauro-BSH clade (predicts bile-acid deconjugation profile).
Cross-reference to any in-vitro survival data at bile 0.3% / pH 2.5 for the strains in the tree.

questions.q: For a candidate probiotic E. faecium strain, what is the minimum experimental protocol to demonstrate a host benefit (as opposed to merely absence of harm), and does the published 17OM39 literature contain any such evidence — e.g. immune modulation (IL-10 induction, Treg expansion), pathogen exclusion (in vitro Salmonella/C. difficile competition, in vivo colonization resistance), SCFA production, or mucin cross-feeding?
questions.basis: The paper's title claims '...key genetic factors associated with probiotic property'. Our replication (REPORT.md §5) confirmed genomic safety features (no vanA/vanB, no functional virulence) but 'safety' and 'probiotic benefit' are two different claims. A strain that is merely non-harmful is a commensal, not a probiotic. The paper does not present host-benefit data; neither can our BV-BRC-only replication. This gap is central to whether 17OM39 has been shown to be a probiotic in the functional sense or merely a safe commensal.
next_steps: Systematic search of any in-vitro (Caco-2/HT-29 co-culture, PBMC cytokine panel) or in-vivo (mouse DSS colitis, mouse Salmonella challenge) studies using 17OM39 since 2018.

Draft a candidate host-benefit assay panel: (a) pathogen exclusion vs C. difficile and VRE in vitro, (b) SCFA production in defined-medium co-culture, (c) IL-10/IL-6/TNFa cytokine panel on PBMCs, (d) 14-day mouse colonization + fecal shedding, (e) mouse DSS colitis rescue endpoint.
Explicitly separate the 'safe' claim (which the paper + our replication support) from the 'probiotic' claim (which requires functional evidence not present in either).
